title: Gathering & Synthesizing Information from Your Team

sections.content:
## What You'll Learn

A team leader or coordinator is constantly in the position of needing information from multiple people simultaneously — weekly status from 8 direct reports, feedback on a proposal from 5 stakeholders, updates on an issue from 3 teams involved. Without structure, this becomes an endless cycle of chasing, consolidating, and re-asking.

Copilot can both collect and synthesize information at scale:
- Send structured update requests to multiple team members simultaneously
- Read and consolidate responses from Slack, Teams, email, or task management systems
- Identify gaps — who hasn't responded, what information is still missing
- Detect conflicts or inconsistencies between what different people have reported
- Generate consolidated reports from multiple sources automatically

This lesson covers the full information lifecycle: requesting → collecting → synthesizing → reporting.

## Requesting Information — The Right Way

Most information requests fail not because people are unwilling to respond, but because the request is unclear about what format, level of detail, or deadline is expected.

### Drafting Structured Update Requests

```
Draft a weekly update request to send to my team of [N] people.
I need to know:
- What they completed this week (specific, not general)
- What they're working on next week
- Any blockers or help needed
- Any risks I should know about

Format requirements:
- Plain text they can reply directly to
- Each item should take 2-3 minutes to fill in
- Clear which fields are mandatory vs. optional
- Explicitly state when I need it by (and time zone)
- One sentence explaining why I'm asking (so they know it's useful, not bureaucratic)

Tone: collegial, not bureaucratic. Maximum 150 words.
```

### Different Request Types

**Stakeholder feedback request:**
```
Draft an email to [stakeholders] requesting feedback on [document/proposal/plan].
What I need: specific feedback on [area 1], [area 2], [area 3].
What I don't need: general comments or editorial feedback.
Deadline: [date and time] — with one sentence on why this deadline.
Format: they can reply directly to this email with numbered responses.
If they have no concerns, a simple 'No issues from my end' is acceptable.
Length: under 100 words — they are busy people.
```

**Information gathering from multiple teams:**
```
I need status information from [Team A], [Team B], and [Team C] about [shared project/issue].
From each team I need:
- Current status of [their workstream]
- Any inter-team dependencies they're waiting on
- Expected completion date

Draft a single message I can adapt and send to each team.
Make it easy to reply with just the facts — not a narrative.
```

## Slack & Microsoft Teams MCP Integration

For teams that communicate primarily via Slack or Teams, connecting Copilot to those systems lets you gather information from conversations without asking anyone to fill in a form.

### Slack MCP Setup

```json
"slack": {
  "command": "npx",
  "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-slack"],
  "env": {
    "SLACK_BOT_TOKEN": "${env:SLACK_TOKEN}",
    "SLACK_TEAM_ID": "${env:SLACK_TEAM_ID}"
  }
}
```

**Requires:** A Slack App with channels:history, channels:read, users:read permissions. Create in api.slack.com/apps.

**Available tools:**
- `list_channels` — list accessible channels
- `get_channel_history` — read messages in a channel
- `get_thread_replies` — read a full thread
- `search_messages` — search across channels
- `post_message` — post a message (use with care)
- `get_user_info` — find a user by name

### Microsoft Teams MCP Setup

```json
"teams": {
  "command": "npx",
  "args": ["-y", "@microsoft/mcp-teams"],
  "env": {
    "M365_TENANT_ID": "${env:M365_TENANT_ID}",
    "M365_ACCESS_TOKEN": "${env:M365_TOKEN}"
  }
}
```

**Government note:** Teams is the standard for many government departments. Your IT team will need to configure the Teams app registration and grant appropriate API permissions. Read permissions are lower risk than post permissions — if you can only get read access approved initially, that's enough for information gathering.

### What You Can Do With Messaging MCP

```
Search [#project-updates] channel for any messages from the last 7 days 
about [topic or project name]. Summarize what each team member reported.
```

```
Read the [#stand-up] channel for the last 5 days. 
For each team member who posted, extract: what they completed, what they're doing next, 
and any blockers mentioned. Format as a team status table.
```

```
Search for any messages mentioning [issue or keyword] across all channels 
I have access to. When was it first mentioned, who raised it, and what was the resolution?
```

## Synthesizing Information from Multiple Sources

Once information is gathered — from task systems, messaging, email, or documents — Copilot can synthesize it into something actionable.

### Multi-Source Synthesis

When you have updates from multiple people (paste all of them into one prompt):

```
I have weekly updates from [N] team members. Synthesize them into:

1. TEAM SUMMARY
   - Overall team health: On Track / Mixed / At Risk
   - What we collectively accomplished this week
   - What we're collectively working on next week

2. ISSUES REQUIRING MY ACTION
   - Any blockers I need to resolve
   - Any decisions people are waiting on
   - Any resource or help requests

3. GAPS
   - Who hasn't submitted an update
   - Any critical information that's missing or unclear

4. ANOMALIES
   - Anything that seems inconsistent between what different people have reported
   - Any reports of the same issue from multiple people (recurring problem signal)

[paste all updates below]
```

### Conflict and Inconsistency Detection

```
I've received these three status updates about the same project from different teams.
Are there any inconsistencies or conflicts in what they're reporting?
Does Team A's update align with what Team B is reporting they're waiting on?
Are there any implicit dependencies that haven't been explicitly acknowledged?

[paste the three updates]
```

### Information Gap Analysis

```
I expected updates from these 8 people: [list names].
I received updates from: [list who responded].
Who hasn't responded? How long have they had to respond?
Draft a brief, friendly follow-up message to the non-respondents.
```

## Building Automated Information Flows

For information you need regularly, build recurring prompts and agent skills that pull it automatically.

### Weekly Status Pull from Multiple Systems

A single agent prompt that synthesizes from task management + messaging:

```
For this week's team status, gather information from multiple sources:

1. From [ADO/Jira]: pull completed and in-progress items for team members [list names]
2. From [Slack #updates channel]: find status updates posted this week by team members
3. From email: search for any replies to last week's status request

Synthesize all sources into a single team status briefing:
- What was accomplished (from all sources combined)
- What's in progress
- Blockers or risks mentioned in any source
- Anything mentioned in one source but absent from others (potential gap)
```

### Feedback Collection and Theme Analysis

When you've collected feedback from multiple people on a proposal, policy, or decision:

```
I received feedback from [N] people on [proposal/document/policy].
Synthesize the feedback:

1. THEMES: What are the 3-5 most common concerns or suggestions?
2. STRONG SUPPORT: What aspects did multiple people praise or agree with?
3. STRONG OPPOSITION: What aspects did multiple people flag as problematic?
4. UNIQUE PERSPECTIVES: Any feedback that was only raised by one person but seems important?
5. CONFLICTS: Did any two people give contradictory feedback on the same point?
6. RECOMMENDATION: Based on the feedback, what changes to the proposal are most warranted?

[paste all feedback below]
```

**Privacy in information synthesis.** When pasting team members' updates, messages, or feedback into Copilot, be aware that this data is sent to AI servers. For government workers:
- Individual performance-related information should be anonymized before pasting (replace names with 'Team Member A', 'B', etc.)
- Sensitive HR matters, personal issues raised in 1:1s, or health-related information should not be processed through AI tools
- Check your organization's acceptable use policy for AI tools before processing any HR or personal data
- Project status data is generally lower risk than people-related data

sections.title: Collect and Synthesize This Week's Team Updates
sections.content:
Apply the full information synthesis workflow to a real current situation.

**Step 1 — Draft update requests** for your team (or for a group you need information from):
```
Draft a weekly status update request for [N] team members.
I need to know: [your specific requirements]
Deadline: [when]
Format: easy to reply to by email or Slack
```

**Step 2 — Collect responses.** If this is for a real team, send the request and wait. For this workshop, you can use past status emails or invent representative responses.

**Step 3 — Paste all responses into one file.** Name it `team-updates-[date].txt`. This file becomes the input.

**Step 4 — Run the synthesis prompt:**
```
Synthesize these [N] weekly team updates into:
1. Team health summary (one sentence)
2. Collective accomplishments this week (bullets)
3. Work in progress (bullets by owner)
4. Issues needing my action (blockers, decisions needed)
5. Information gaps (who's missing, what's unclear)
6. Anomalies (inconsistencies between people's reports)
```

**Step 5 — Generate the upward report:**
```
From the synthesized team status, write a 3-paragraph manager update:
- Paragraph 1: What the team accomplished
- Paragraph 2: What's in progress and any risks
- Paragraph 3: What I need from leadership (or 'No items requiring leadership action')
```

**Assess:** How much time did collecting + synthesizing + reporting take with Copilot vs. doing it manually? What would you improve in the collection process to make the synthesis cleaner?

sections.title: Workshop A — Feedback Synthesis
sections.content:
Synthesize feedback from multiple people on a real document, proposal, or policy.

**Choose a real item** that you've received or will receive feedback on:
- A policy document
- A project proposal
- A process change
- A report draft
- A proposed solution to a problem

**Step 1 — Collect feedback.** If you don't have feedback yet, describe the document and create representative feedback from 4-5 hypothetical stakeholders with different perspectives.

**Step 2 — Run the feedback synthesis prompt:**
```
Synthesize this feedback from [N] stakeholders on [document/proposal name].

1. Top 3 themes (what multiple people mentioned)
2. What's universally supported
3. What's universally opposed
4. Contradictory feedback (where two people disagree)
5. Unique important concerns (only one person raised but significant)
6. Recommended changes to address the most important feedback

[paste all feedback]
```

**Step 3 — Create a response plan:**
```
Based on the synthesis, which feedback items will I:
- Address in the next revision (high importance, reasonable to act on)
- Acknowledge but not change (understand the concern, but we're not changing it — explain why)
- Defer to a later version
- Decline (outside scope or contradicts core objective)

Create a brief response table: FEEDBACK | RESPONSE | RATIONALE
```

**Step 4 — Draft a response summary** to send back to all who provided feedback, explaining what you're changing and why some suggestions weren't incorporated.

**Outcome:** A professional, thorough stakeholder response process that respects everyone's input while making clear decisions.

sections.title: Workshop B — Slack/Teams Information Extraction
sections.content:
Use messaging MCP to gather team information without sending a single request.

**Option A — With Slack MCP:**

**Step 1 — Set up the Slack MCP** (if not done in lesson 6-17).

**Step 2 — Information extraction prompts:**
```
Search the #[project-channel] channel for the last 14 days.
Extract: any status updates, decisions mentioned, blockers raised, 
and action items that were agreed upon in thread conversations.
Format as a structured summary.
```

```
Search all channels I have access to for messages about [specific topic or project].
Group by: person who mentioned it, date, what they said.
Are there any conflicts in what different people are saying about this topic?
```

**Option B — Without MCP (paste-based):**
Export a Slack or Teams conversation (copy the text) and paste into Copilot Chat:
```
From this Teams/Slack conversation thread:
1. Who are the participants and what is each person's position?
2. What decisions were made (named decision + who made it)?
3. What action items were agreed (named person + task + deadline)?
4. What's unresolved?
5. What would a new person reading this need to know to get up to speed in 60 seconds?
```

**Step 3 — Compare to what you knew manually.** Did Copilot surface anything from the conversation that you had forgotten or missed?

sections.title: Workshop C — Build a Team Information System
sections.content:
Design and build a repeatable information flow for your team — a system that makes information collection and synthesis a routine, not a chore.

**Design your system by answering:**

**What information do you need regularly?**
- Weekly: [list what you need every week]
- Monthly: [list what you need monthly]
- Event-triggered: [list what you need when something specific happens]

**Who provides each type of information?**
- Direct reports: [what they provide]
- Peer teams: [what they provide]
- Leadership: [what they provide]

**Where does the information currently live?**
- Task systems (ADO/Jira/GitHub): [what's here]
- Messaging (Slack/Teams): [what's here]
- Email: [what's here]
- Documents: [what's here]

**Build these artifacts:**

1. **Weekly update request template** (`email-weekly-update-request.prompt.md`) — what you send every week, customized for your team

2. **Information synthesis prompt** (`team-status-synthesis.prompt.md`) — what you run when all updates are in

3. **Gap chaser template** (`email-update-reminder.prompt.md`) — the follow-up to non-responders (friendly but clear)

4. **Upward report template** (`email-upward-status.prompt.md`) — turning synthesized team data into a manager update

5. **MCP pull prompt** (if available) — pulling data from your task system to supplement team updates

**Run the full cycle once** with real data from your team.

**Outcome:** An information system where the collection, synthesis, and reporting happen in under 30 minutes each week — instead of consuming most of your Monday morning.

sections.question: You receive 7 weekly updates from your team members. Three of them mention that the deployment pipeline is slow, using different words ('pipeline is taking forever', 'builds are slow', 'CI is a bottleneck'). What should Copilot identify this as in a synthesis?
options: A theme — the same underlying problem surfacing independently in multiple people's updates, which signals it is a real systemic issue worth addressing, not a one-off complaint
Noise — since they're describing it differently, they probably mean different things
A blocker affecting only the three people who mentioned it
sections.explanation: When multiple people independently report the same issue using different words, that's a signal — not noise. In synthesis, this pattern is called a theme: a concern that appears across multiple sources without coordination. The fact that three people used different phrasings actually strengthens the signal — they each noticed it independently, so it's a genuine systemic problem. In your synthesis prompt, asking specifically for 'recurring issues mentioned by multiple people' helps Copilot surface these themes rather than treating them as three separate data points.

sections.question: You want to paste six team members' weekly updates into Copilot for synthesis. One update from a team member mentions they had a personal health issue that affected their productivity this week. Should you include this in what you paste?
options: Yes — include everything for the most accurate synthesis
No — anonymize or remove personal health information before pasting to AI tools. Synthesize the work-related parts only.
Yes, but ask Copilot to ignore personal details
Only if you have the person's permission
sections.explanation: Personal health information is sensitive data and should not be sent to AI tools under most government and enterprise data handling policies. Before pasting team updates for synthesis, review each one and remove or anonymize any personal health information, mental health mentions, family situations, or other HR-sensitive content. The AI doesn't need to know why someone's productivity was affected — it only needs to know the work-related output and plans. Handle personal information through appropriate HR channels, not AI synthesis tools.

sections.content: **Lesson 6-26 complete.** Information synthesis is where Copilot provides disproportionate value — pulling together fragmented, inconsistent data from multiple sources into a clear picture takes humans hours and is easily missed. Copilot can do it in minutes and will flag gaps and conflicts you'd have missed. Combined with structured collection (lesson) and automated reporting (lesson 6-27), this creates an intelligence layer that makes your team's work transparent without requiring anyone to do extra reporting work. Lesson 6-27 covers stakeholder communication — writing for every audience level, from team members to ministers.
